title: Hansen Disease

steps.tx: **Mycobacterium leprae** is an obligate, acid-fast, intracellular bacillus with a unique tropism for cooler peripheral body tissues, specifically skin histiocytes and peripheral nerve Schwann cells. Possessing an exceptionally long doubling time of twelve to fourteen days, it cannot be cultured on artificial cell-free media. Inoculation occurs through respiratory droplets from untreated lepromatous patients during prolonged household contact. The pathogen enters Schwann cells via phenolic glycolipid-1 binding to laminin-2 on the basal lamina.
steps.say: Mycobacterium leprae is an acid-fast intracellular rod that targets cooler skin areas and Schwann cells. It doubles slowly every twelve to fourteen days and cannot be cultured in vitro, relying on phenolic glycolipid-1 to invade peripheral nerves.

steps.tx: **Ridley-Jopling classification** categorizes leprosy along a five-group immunological spectrum determined entirely by the host cell-mediated immune response against the bacillus. At the hyper-reactive pole lies tuberculoid leprosy (TT), characterised by high cell-mediated immunity and scarce bacilli. At the anergic pole lies lepromatous leprosy (LL), marked by absent cell-mediated immunity, unrestrained bacillary proliferation, and high humoral antibody titres. Unstable intermediate groups comprise borderline tuberculoid (BT), mid-borderline (BB), and borderline lepromatous (BL) disease.
steps.say: The Ridley-Jopling classification spans from polar tuberculoid with strong immunity and few lesions, through borderline categories, down to anergic lepromatous leprosy with diffuse bacillary proliferation and negative lepromin skin tests.

vis.alt: Diagram illustrating the Ridley-Jopling spectrum of leprosy and immune responses.
vis.caption: The Ridley-Jopling immunological spectrum from polar tuberculoid to polar lepromatous disease. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: **Cardinal signs** defined by the World Health Organization establish the clinical diagnosis of leprosy when at least one of three criteria is present: a hypopigmented or erythematous skin lesion with definite loss of sensation; thickened or enlarged peripheral nerve trunks with corresponding sensory impairment or motor weakness; and a positive slit-skin smear demonstrating acid-fast bacilli. Testing for sensory impairment must methodically evaluate light touch with a wisp of cotton wool, temperature discrimination, and pinprick pain.
steps.say: The diagnosis of leprosy requires at least one WHO cardinal sign: an anaesthetic hypopigmented macule, thickened peripheral nerves with weakness, or positive acid-fast bacilli on slit-skin smear. Always test temperature and light touch systematically.

steps.tx: **Lepromatous leprosy** exhibits widespread, symmetrical, bilateral cutaneous infiltration characterized by multiple shiny macules, papules, nodules, and plaques with ill-defined borders. Facial dermal thickening and deep furrowing create classic leonine facies, accompanied by madarosis or loss of lateral eyebrows, and destruction of nasal septal cartilage producing saddle nose deformity. Peripheral nerve enlargement is diffuse and symmetrical. Dermal histiocytes become laden with ingested lipids and packed with globi of acid-fast bacilli, forming pathognomonic Virchow cells.
steps.say: Lepromatous leprosy produces symmetrical facial infiltration, giving leonine facies, loss of eyebrows, and saddle nose deformity. Dermal histiocytes fill with lipid and dense clusters of bacilli known as globi, creating pathognomonic Virchow cells.

steps.tx: **Type 1 lepra reaction** represents a delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction occurring exclusively in borderline forms (BT, BB, BL) during or following antimicrobial therapy. Driven by acute enhancement of cell-mediated immunity against mycobacterial antigens, existing skin plaques become suddenly erythematous, swollen, and tender. More critically, acute painful inflammation of peripheral nerve trunks (acute neuritis) rapidly supervenes, threatening irreversible axonal destruction and sudden claw hand or foot drop. High-dose oral prednisolone initiated immediately arrests neural destruction.
steps.say: A type one lepra reaction is a delayed hypersensitivity flare in borderline leprosy. Existing skin patches turn red and swollen, but acute neuritis is the real emergency. Immediate high-dose oral corticosteroids are required to prevent permanent claw hand deformities.

steps.tx: **Erythema nodosum leprosum** constitutes a type 2 lepra reaction mediated by circulating immune-complex deposition in multibacillary patients (BL and LL). Patients develop explosive crops of painful, tender, erythematous subcutaneous nodules accompanied by high remittent fever, malaise, lymphadenopathy, and polyarthritis. Severe systemic vasculitis can induce iridocyclitis, orchitis, dactylitis, and immune-complex glomerulonephritis. Thalidomide administered at one hundred to four hundred milligrams daily acts as the most potent therapy by suppressing tumour necrosis factor-alpha.
steps.say: Type two reaction, or erythema nodosum leprosum, is an immune-complex vasculitis in lepromatous patients. It causes painful red nodules, fever, and orchitis. Thalidomide is the drug of choice, working rapidly by inhibiting TNF-alpha.

steps.tx: **Slit-skin smear** provides essential semi-quantitative microbiological assessment of bacillary density. Fluid scraped from the dermis of both earlobes, the forehead, and active skin lesions is heat-fixed and stained using the Ziehl-Neelsen technique with five percent sulfuric acid rather than twenty percent, reflecting the weaker acid-fastness of M. leprae. The bacterial index (BI) is graded on a logarithmic scale from 0 to 6+, where 6+ indicates more than one thousand bacilli per microscopic oil-immersion field.
steps.say: Slit-skin smears taken from earlobes and lesions use five percent sulfuric acid for decolourisation because lepra bacilli are less acid-fast than tubercle bacilli. The bacterial index scores bacillary density on a scale from zero to six plus.

steps.tx: **Multidrug therapy** protocols mandated by the World Health Organization eliminate bacillary transmission and prevent the emergence of drug resistance. Paucibacillary leprosy with one to five skin lesions receives six months of supervised monthly rifampicin 600 mg plus daily self-administered dapsone 100 mg. Multibacillary leprosy with six or more lesions receives twelve months of triple therapy: supervised monthly rifampicin 600 mg and clofazimine 300 mg, accompanied by daily self-administered dapsone 100 mg and clofazimine 50 mg.
steps.say: WHO multidrug therapy prevents drug resistance: paucibacillary disease receives six months of monthly rifampicin and daily dapsone; multibacillary disease receives twelve months of triple therapy adding clofazimine to rifampicin and dapsone.
